question: Prove that if a real-valued function $f$ is differentiable at a point $x=c$, then $f$ must be continuous at $x=c$, using the definition of differentiability and the corresponding limit.

options.A: Differentiability at $c$ gives $\lim_{x\to c}f(x)=f'(c)$, so $f$ is continuous at $c$.
options.B: Since $f'(c)=\lim_{x\to c}\frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c}$ is finite, $\lim_{x\to c}[f(x)-f(c)]=f'(c)\cdot0=0$, hence $\lim_{x\to c}f(x)=f(c)$.
options.C: Since $\lim_{x\to c}(x-c)=0$, the difference quotient must be zero, so $f(c)=0$ and $f$ is continuous.
options.D: Differentiability at $c$ implies $\lim_{x\to c}f(x)=0$, which equals $f(c)$ for every differentiable function.
